tur51-0: In a Cochrane review of studies in older people living in the community, exercise reduced the number of falls by 23% and the number of people who fell by 15%. Exercises that train balance and everyday movements reduced the number of falls by 24%; programmes combining these with strengthening exercises probably reduce the number of falls by 34% (moderate-certainty evidence). Tai Chi can also reduce falls.
tur51-1: A 2022 Cochrane review of 40 studies and 4,059 people found that exercises focused on walking, balance and everyday tasks improve mobility. In programmes after discharge from hospital, the improvement in mobility was small but meaningful, and the evidence was of high certainty; strength exercises in this period may also help (low-certainty evidence).
tur51-2: Yes. A Cochrane review of 40 studies showed that exercises focused on walking, balance and everyday tasks after leaving hospital clearly improve mobility. In a US study of 232 patients, a 6-month home exercise programme improved function further, even in patients who had already completed rehabilitation. Not every programme is equally effective: in the CAP trial of 210 patients, at the end of a 16-week home programme the proportion reaching the threshold for independent walking in the community (more than 300 metres in 6 minutes) was 23% in the group doing aerobic, strength and balance exercise and 18% in the group receiving range-of-motion exercises and electrical nerve stimulation. The difference was not significant; in both groups the average walking distance increased from the start.
tur51-3: According to a review published in the journal JAMA in 2022, the first treatment is adjusting your activity, pain control and physiotherapy. In a US study of 259 patients with an average age of 72, manual therapy combined with an individual exercise programme improved symptoms and walking capacity at 2 months more than medical care (medication or epidural injections) or group exercise. At 6 months there was no difference between the groups; walking distance had increased from the start in all three.
tur51-4: In another study, 169 patients who were candidates for surgery were assigned either to surgery (decompression) or to a standard physiotherapy programme. After 2 years there was no meaningful difference in physical function between the two groups; however, more than half (57%) of the patients in the physiotherapy group had surgery during that time. A Cochrane review of five studies (643 patients) states that no firm conclusion can be drawn on whether surgery or non-surgical treatment is better; complications occurred in 10–24% of those who had surgery, while no side effects were reported for the non-surgical treatments.
